title: Medication × weather safety
description: Baked medication/supplement × WEATHER safety dataset (issue #1727) — the curated attribute lists behind two compositions: PHOTOSENSITIZING items (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, thiazides, amiodarone, systemic retinoids, sulfonamides, some NSAIDs, voriconazole, St John's Wort) enrich the existing high-UV line, and HEAT-RISK items (diuretics, anticholinergics, beta-blockers, stimulants, antipsychotics, SGLT2 inhibitors) enrich the heatwave line. Items match by RxNorm ingredient CUI + synonym (the shared machinery) and the check is KIND-BLIND — a supplement can be a photosensitizer. INFORMATIONAL, never prescriptive; the absence of a flag is NOT clearance (a curated subset). Fully OFFLINE. Committed + HUMAN-REVIEWABLE; regenerate with `npm run gen:weather-med-safety`.

citation.source: U.S. FDA — The Sun and Your Medicine (drug-induced photosensitivity)
citation.note: Uncopyrightable clinical facts (these drug classes cause photosensitivity) stated in our own words and cited to the FDA consumer reference. Drug generic/brand names are public nomenclature.

citation.source: U.S. NLM DailyMed — FDA-approved labeling (photosensitivity warnings)
citation.note: Photosensitivity warnings appear in the FDA-approved labeling for these agents; facts restated in our own words.

citation.source: U.S. CDC — Heat and Medications / Heat-Related Illness guidance
citation.note: Public-health guidance that these medication classes raise heat-illness risk, stated in our own words.

citation.source: U.S. NIH NIA — Hot Weather Safety for Older Adults; CDC heat guidance
citation.note: NIH consumer guidance on heat risk including medication effects, stated in our own words.

citation.source: U.S. NIH NCCIH — St. John's Wort; DailyMed labeling (photosensitivity)
citation.note: NIH reference for St John's Wort, including increased sun sensitivity; stated in our own words.

entries.label: Amiodarone
entries.note: Amiodarone causes photosensitivity in a substantial share of people taking it, and prolonged exposure can leave lasting skin discoloration.
entries.source: U.S. NLM DailyMed — FDA-approved labeling (photosensitivity warnings)

entries.label: Anticholinergics (sedating antihistamines, tricyclics, oxybutynin)
entries.note: Anticholinergic medicines reduce sweating, which is the body's main way of shedding heat.
entries.source: U.S. CDC — Heat and Medications / Heat-Related Illness guidance

entries.label: Antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine)
entries.note: Antipsychotics can interfere with the brain's temperature regulation and with sweating, raising heat-illness risk in a hot spell.
entries.source: U.S. CDC — Heat and Medications / Heat-Related Illness guidance

entries.label: Beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol)
entries.clause: can blunt the body's heat response
entries.note: Beta-blockers blunt the increase in heart rate and skin blood flow the body uses to shed heat, so hot weather is harder to compensate for.
entries.source: U.S. NIH NIA — Hot Weather Safety for Older Adults; CDC heat guidance

entries.label: Diuretics (loop and thiazide)
entries.clause: can add to dehydration risk in heat
entries.note: Diuretics increase fluid loss, which compounds the dehydration a hot spell already causes.
entries.source: U.S. CDC — Heat and Medications / Heat-Related Illness guidance

entries.label: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin)
entries.note: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics carry a labeled photosensitivity warning; sun exposure during a course can produce an exaggerated sunburn reaction.
entries.source: U.S. NLM DailyMed — FDA-approved labeling (photosensitivity warnings)

entries.label: Photosensitizing NSAIDs (piroxicam, naproxen)
entries.note: Some NSAIDs — piroxicam and naproxen most notably — are documented photosensitizers, unlike the class as a whole.
entries.source: U.S. FDA — The Sun and Your Medicine (drug-induced photosensitivity)

entries.label: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
entries.clause: can add to dehydration risk in heat
entries.note: SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary fluid loss, which adds to the dehydration risk of a hot spell.
entries.source: U.S. CDC — Heat and Medications / Heat-Related Illness guidance

entries.label: St John's Wort
entries.note: St John's Wort can increase sensitivity to sunlight, particularly at higher doses — a supplement with a drug-like photosensitizing effect.
entries.source: U.S. NIH NCCIH — St. John's Wort; DailyMed labeling (photosensitivity)

entries.label: Stimulants (amphetamines, methylphenidate)
entries.note: Stimulants raise body heat production and can mask the tiredness that would otherwise be a cue to stop.
entries.source: U.S. CDC — Heat and Medications / Heat-Related Illness guidance

entries.label: Sulfonamide antibacterials (sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim)
entries.note: Sulfonamide antibacterials carry a labeled photosensitivity warning.
entries.source: U.S. NLM DailyMed — FDA-approved labeling (photosensitivity warnings)

entries.label: Systemic retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin)
entries.note: Systemic retinoids thin the outer skin layer and are labeled for increased sensitivity to sunlight.
entries.source: U.S. NLM DailyMed — FDA-approved labeling (photosensitivity warnings)

entries.label: Tetracycline antibiotics (doxycycline, minocycline, tetracycline)
entries.note: Tetracycline antibiotics — doxycycline most of all — are among the best-documented causes of drug-induced photosensitivity: skin can burn faster and at lower sun exposure than usual.
entries.source: U.S. FDA — The Sun and Your Medicine (drug-induced photosensitivity)

entries.label: Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone)
entries.note: Thiazide diuretics, hydrochlorothiazide in particular, are a well-documented cause of drug-induced photosensitivity with long-term use.
entries.source: U.S. FDA — The Sun and Your Medicine (drug-induced photosensitivity)

entries.label: Voriconazole
entries.note: Voriconazole causes marked photosensitivity, and its labeling advises avoiding strong direct sunlight during treatment.
entries.source: U.S. NLM DailyMed — FDA-approved labeling (photosensitivity warnings)
